standard.title: Sentences express ideas
standard.description: recognise that sentences are key units for expressing ideas
standard.prior_knowledge: Students use spoken sentences naturally but have not yet reflected on what makes a sentence. They have not yet been asked to distinguish a sentence from a fragment or to identify word order as meaningful.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students can identify a sentence as a complete unit that expresses a single idea, distinguish it from a fragment, and recognise that word order affects meaning.

nodes.label: A sentence is complete
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify that a sentence expresses a complete idea — it makes sense on its own.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify whether a group of words is a complete sentence or a fragment in one example.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise the difference between a sentence fragment and a complete sentence; identify sentences in familiar texts; understand that a sentence expresses a single complete idea.
wider: Sort a range of written phrases and sentences into 'complete' and 'not complete' groups and explain the sorting
Identify sentences and fragments across different text types — labels, books, signs — comparing how completeness shows up in different contexts
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding that a sentence is a complete unit is a prerequisite for Node 2 — students cannot reason about word order affecting sentence meaning if they do not yet have a concept of what a sentence is as a unit.

response_modes.reason: The sentence/fragment distinction can feel arbitrary when only one or two examples are used. Multiple contrasting pairs help build the concept of 'completeness' as a stable criterion.

success_criteria: Student can identify a sentence as expressing a complete idea.
Student can say why a fragment does not make sense on its own.

nodes.label: Word order carries meaning
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can demonstrate that changing word order in a sentence changes — or destroys — its meaning.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify that two sentences with the same words in different order mean different things (e.g. 'The boy sat on the dog' vs 'The dog sat on the boy').
nodes.typical_width: Understand that word order in sentences is important for meaning; experiment with reordering words in simple sentences and observe what happens to meaning.
wider: Create multiple sentences from a small set of words in different orders — exploring which orders make sense and which don't
Compare word order in English sentences with word order in other languages familiar to students in the class

response_modes.reason: Students may think order is arbitrary or that meaning comes only from individual words. Multiple examples — including deliberately nonsensical reorderings — are needed to consolidate that word order is systematically meaningful in English.

success_criteria: Student can explain that moving words around in a sentence changes what it means.
Student can produce or identify at least one example of the same words in different order making different sense.
